title: The Night the Sensors Saved the Fish: Aquaponics Monitoring in Practice
subtitle: A near-miss oxygen crash, a 3am Telegram alert, and what we learned about the difference between logging data and acting on it
author: domingo-altamirano
body_text:
On the night of August 14th, at 3:17am, my phone sent me a Telegram message that said: DO ALERT: Zone Aquaponics Bay — dissolved oxygen 4.1 ppm, threshold 5.0. The alert had been configured for about six months but had never triggered. I stared at it for a moment, convinced it was a false positive from the sensor, then got up and went to the bay.

The water was milky. Not dramatically — you had to look for it — but turbid in a way it wasn't supposed to be. The aerator was running. The circulation pump sounded normal. But the DO probe was reading 4.0 and dropping.

I spent the next 90 minutes running a second aerator from the equipment room, checking the primary aerator diffuser (partially fouled — I cleaned it), doing a manual DO check with our handheld meter (confirmed: 3.9 at its lowest, sensor was correct), and watching the numbers come back up. By 5am we were at 5.8 and climbing.

220 tilapia almost died. They didn't, because a sensor sent me a message.

I want to document this incident carefully, not because it was a triumph of our monitoring system — though it was that — but because the 90 minutes I spent in the bay that night exposed some gaps in our monitoring design that I think are worth examining publicly.

**What We Had**

The Tide monitoring system tracks seven water quality parameters in the aquaponics bay. Everything logs to InfluxDB every 5 minutes. We have a Grafana dashboard that anyone with our local network access can view. We had configured Telegram alerts for pH outside 6.5–7.8 and DO below 5.0 ppm. Beyond that, we had mostly assumed that as long as the pump was running and the aerator was running, things were fine.

This is the wrong mental model for aquaponics. The system is biological, not mechanical. The biofilter is a living community of nitrifying bacteria. The fish are breathing. The plants are transpiring. A system where the equipment is running can still be failing biologically.

**What We Didn't Have (Until That Night)**

We had no alert for rapid rate-of-change. Looking at the logs after the fact, the DO had been declining for approximately 3.5 hours before it hit the threshold. The decline was gradual enough that each individual 5-minute reading looked reasonable compared to the one before it. But the 3.5-hour trend was obvious. If we'd had a rate-of-change alert — flag if DO drops more than X ppm over Y hours — we'd have had a two-hour earlier warning.

We also had no alert for the combination of conditions that preceded the crash. The turbidity reading had been elevated for almost 6 hours (a bacterial bloom — we think from a high-protein feed batch that decomposed faster than normal). High turbidity implies high biological oxygen demand. Our individual-parameter alerting couldn't see that combination as meaningful.

And we had no overnight staffing protocol. What if I hadn't woken up? What if I'd ignored the message? We rely on a single person receiving an alert and acting on it in the middle of the night. That is not a robust system.

**Changes We Made**

Rate-of-change alerts: We now alert on any DO drop greater than 0.8 ppm in a 2-hour window, regardless of absolute level. This is a leading indicator rather than a lagging one. Since implementation, it's triggered twice — once for real (a partial pump failure that we caught and fixed before crisis) and once for a sensor recalibration event that looked like a real decline.

Combined condition monitoring: Priya helped us build a simple rule-based monitor that checks for conditions that together are higher risk than any one of them alone: elevated turbidity + declining DO + recent feeding event. It's not ML, it's just an OR gate on three conditions. But it would have flagged our August event four hours earlier.

Notification redundancy: Critical alerts now go to a three-person rotation, not just me. If the primary doesn't acknowledge within 15 minutes, it escalates to the next. We tested this protocol and discovered that two of the three people's phones were in Do Not Disturb overnight modes that would have silenced the original alert. We changed that.

Backup aeration: We now have a second aerator plumbed and ready to run immediately, triggered manually by a wall switch next to the bay door. Before, the backup aerator was in the equipment room on a shelf, requiring me to find it, find the hosing, and connect it. Ninety seconds versus fifteen minutes in an emergency.

**The Philosophical Part**

I think a lot about the difference between monitoring and operational readiness. We had excellent monitoring. We had mediocre operational readiness. The monitoring told us there was a problem; the operational readiness determined whether we could respond effectively to that knowledge.

The sensor system did its job. Everything else — the alert design, the notification protocol, the response procedure — was our job, and it was partially incomplete. We got lucky that the gap was covered by me waking up at 3am and taking a message seriously.

The 220 tilapia are fine. They've been fed and counted daily since the incident. They don't know anything happened. I remain grateful for that, and for the somewhat overbuilt sensor array that Anouk and I argued over in the original system design — she wanted fewer sensors and simpler logging; I wanted more sensors and richer data. In this case, the richer data would have given us earlier warning if we'd been using it correctly. Neither of us was fully right. We're both right now.

title: Four Years In: What We Expected, What We Found
subtitle: A collective reflection from the founding members on the gaps between our original assumptions and what running an experimental robotics homestead actually looks like
author: nkechi-obi-solomon
body_text:
Cassius and I started talking about this project in 2019, during a period when we were both living and working in ways that felt increasingly disconnected from things that mattered to us. We had a vague vision: a community of technically-skilled people applying those skills to regenerative land use, operating transparently, sharing what they learned. The specifics took years to fill in.

In July 2020, seven of us moved onto the property. In October 2024, we're 40 people, plus seasonal members, plus a visitor program, plus an increasingly active online community following our work. I want to mark that four-year point honestly — not with a press release, but with an accounting.

**What We Expected: Technology Would Be the Hard Part**

When Cassius, Tobias, and I were doing early planning, we spent most of our time on technical questions. What's the soil type? How much solar capacity? What robotics stack? What communication protocols? The assumption was that getting the technology right would be the defining challenge.

We were wrong in a specific way: the technology is hard, but it is tractable in the way that engineering problems are tractable. You can iterate on a robot. You can retrain a model. You can replace a sensor that fails. The progress is visible and the feedback loops are short.

The community dynamics have been harder, in ways that are less visible and have longer feedback loops. Forty people living and working together, making collective decisions about resources and direction and conflict — this is where most of our real difficulty has lived. Not in the soil sensors. In the meeting where two people who both care deeply about the farm disagree about how to use it, and both of them are right.

**What We Expected: Clear Separation Between Technology Experiments and Community Life**

We imagined a fairly clean division: the farm is managed via automation and human oversight; the community lives alongside that with normal social structures. In practice, the technology decisions and the community decisions are inseparable.

When we decided to automate the coop rotation, we were also deciding that two members' daily task of moving the coop manually was no longer needed. That sounds like an efficiency improvement; it was also a disruption to the routine those members had structured their mornings around, and an implicit statement about what kinds of contributions the community values. We didn't think about it that way before we deployed the system. We had to think about it afterward.

We now have a governance principle we didn't have at the start: any automation that eliminates a meaningful community task requires a community decision, not just a technical decision. The criteria aren't just efficiency — they include asking what the task was doing for the people doing it.

**What We Found: The Documentation Became as Important as the Experiments**

Anouk joined in 2021 with the explicit brief of making sure we documented our experiments properly. We thought this was a supporting function — a way to capture knowledge for internal use and share it externally.

It turned out to be core. The discipline of writing down what we were doing, why, and what happened has changed the quality of our thinking about experiments. You can't write a clear account of a poorly designed experiment without noticing the problems. The documentation process improved the experiments by requiring us to articulate them precisely.

The public journal has also created relationships with people and communities we'd never have met otherwise. Researchers who share data with us. Other communities who are running parallel experiments and want to compare notes. Students who read our failure reports and reach out. The openness has given back more than it cost.

**What We Found: 40 People Is Its Own Kind of System**

One of the pleasures of this work, which I didn't fully anticipate, is watching the community develop its own emergent properties. Patterns that nobody designed. Relationships that the governance documents don't capture. Informal expertise-sharing that happens in the kitchen at breakfast.

We have members who arrived as robotics engineers and became passionate composters. Members who arrived as permaculture designers and taught themselves embedded systems. The crossover is real and it changes how people approach problems — an engineer who has spent a season composting thinks about biological system failure modes differently than one who hasn't.

**The Honest Accounting**

Things that have gone worse than expected: community growth has been harder to manage than we anticipated. We've gotten better at it but the learning curve for new members is steep, and we've had people leave who didn't fit, which is always painful. The technology has also been more expensive than initial projections — hardware costs, failure rates, the labor of skilled people maintaining complex systems.

Things that have gone better than expected: food production yields are significantly above our projections. The knowledge-sharing culture has been stronger and more generative than we hoped. The external relationships — with researchers, other communities, visitors — have exceeded what we imagined for a project this size.

Things we still don't know: whether any of this is replicable. Our specific combination of people, place, skills, and timing may not generalize to a model that others can copy. We hope it does. We're trying to document it carefully enough that people can try. But we're aware that we might just be lucky in ways we don't fully understand.

Come visit. Look at the actual soil. Talk to actual people. Ask hard questions. That's the best documentation we have.
